title: NLP Fundamentals
blurb: Tests bag of words and TF-IDF, the distributional hypothesis behind word embeddings, subword tokenisation and why it removes out-of-vocabulary words, perplexity, the step from static to contextual embeddings, and why TF-IDF beat averaged GloVe vectors on topic classification.

ideas.title: Word embeddings and the distributional hypothesis

refLinks.label: §27.2.2 Word Embeddings and the Distributional Hypothesis

questions.prompt: What does bag of words throw away?
options: Word counts. It keeps only the order in which the words first appear.
Rare words. It keeps only the most common ones.
Word order and grammar. It keeps only how often each word appears.
Nothing. It is a lossless encoding of the text.
questions.explanation: "the cat sat on the mat" becomes {the: 2, cat: 1, sat: 1, on: 1, mat: 1}. Order and grammar are gone, and counts are kept. It still works well for classification where word presence matters more than sequence.

questions.prompt: What problem with raw bag of words does TF-IDF fix?
options: Word order is lost, so "not good" looks like "good".
Common words like "the" dominate every document's vector, whatever the topic.
Synonyms like "car" and "automobile" get separate, unrelated dimensions in the vector.
Words outside the vocabulary are dropped.
questions.explanation: The IDF factor down-weights words found in most documents and up-weights rare, informative ones. TF-IDF still treats synonyms as unrelated and still ignores order. Embeddings address synonymy, and subword tokenisation addresses unknown words.

questions.prompt: A word appears in every one of 1,000 documents. What is its IDF, using log(N / df)?
questions.explanation: IDF = log(1000 / 1000) = log(1) = 0. A word present everywhere carries no information about which document you are in, so TF-IDF gives it zero weight.

questions.prompt: A word appears 3 times in a 100-word document. It appears in 10 of the corpus's 1,000 documents. Using TF = count / document length and IDF = ln(N / df), what is its TF-IDF weight? Give three decimal places.
What is the distributional hypothesis that word embeddings are trained on?
options: Words with similar spellings or shared roots tend to mean similar things.
Each word's meaning is fixed by a dictionary definition.
Words that appear near the same neighbours tend to mean similar things.
Words that appear more often carry more meaning.
questions.explanation: "You shall know a word by the company it keeps" (Firth, 1957). The training signal is context. Frequency and spelling are not the basis, and no dictionary is involved.

questions.prompt: How do Word2Vec's Skip-gram and CBOW objectives differ?
options: Skip-gram predicts the word from its context. CBOW predicts the context from a word.
Skip-gram predicts the context from a word. CBOW predicts the word from its whole context.
Skip-gram trains on a co-occurrence matrix. CBOW trains on sentences.
Skip-gram uses characters. CBOW uses whole words.
questions.explanation: The chapter gives Skip-gram as predict context from word, and CBOW (continuous bag of words) as predict word from context. Training on a corpus-wide co-occurrence matrix is GloVe's approach.

questions.prompt: Why does king − man + woman land near queen in an embedding space?
options: The embedding was trained on a long list of analogies, so it memorised this one exactly.
The vectors were hand-edited by linguists to make analogies work.
Co-occurrence statistics encode relations, which show up as consistent vector offsets.
It is a coincidence of one query, which other analogies don't repeat.
questions.explanation: The chapter says this isn't magic. It emerges from co-occurrence statistics. The worked example also shows paris − france + italy returning rome, with the next four all real Italian or nearby European cities, so it is not one lucky query.

questions.prompt: In the worked example's analogy search, why are king, man and woman excluded from the results?
options: They are not in the 400,000-word GloVe vocabulary.
Their vectors are all zero after the subtraction.
Cosine similarity can't be computed for words that are used in the query itself.
The result stays near its inputs, so king itself would usually top the list.
questions.explanation: king − man + woman is still near king, so without excluding the inputs the nearest word is often king itself. The comment in Listing 27.8 notes the exclusion. The words are in the vocabulary, and cosine similarity works for any non-zero vector.

questions.prompt: How does Byte-Pair Encoding build its vocabulary?
options: It assigns one token to every word in a dictionary.
It starts from characters and keeps merging the most frequent adjacent pair.
It groups words by meaning and gives each group a token.
It starts from whole words and keeps splitting the rarest ones in half until none are rare.
questions.explanation: BPE merges the most frequent adjacent pair thousands of times until it reaches the target vocabulary size. Common words end up as one token, and rare words split into known pieces.

questions.prompt: Why does subword tokenisation remove the out-of-vocabulary problem?
options: It maps every unknown word to one shared <unk> token, which the model learns to read.
Any string breaks into known pieces, down to single characters or bytes if needed.
It ignores any word it hasn't seen before.
It retrains the vocabulary each time a new word appears.
questions.explanation: Because characters or bytes are in the vocabulary, every input decomposes into something known. A shared <unk> token is the old fix the chapter criticises, since it throws away the word's signal.

questions.prompt: What does SentencePiece drop that BPE and WordPiece usually assume?
options: That the vocabulary has a fixed size
That tokens map to integer IDs
That common words become single tokens
That spaces mark word boundaries
questions.explanation: SentencePiece treats the input as a raw stream, so it works for languages that don't separate words with spaces. It still has a fixed vocabulary, still merges common words, and still maps tokens to IDs.

questions.prompt: A language model assigns probabilities 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 to the three real tokens of a held-out text. What is its perplexity on that text?
questions.explanation: Perplexity is exp of the average negative log-likelihood. NLLs are ln 2, ln 4 and ln 8, which average (1 + 2 + 3) ln 2 / 3 = 2 ln 2. exp(2 ln 2) = 4. That is the geometric mean of 1/p: the model was as surprised as if picking from 4 equal options.

questions.prompt: What does it mean that GloVe and Word2Vec embeddings are static?
options: A word has one vector in every sentence, so river "bank" and loan "bank" look the same.
The vectors can't be loaded once training ends.
The vectors never change their size, unlike the contextual embeddings inside a transformer.
The vectors only work for nouns.
questions.explanation: One vector per word, whatever the context. Transformers replace this with contextual embeddings, computed from the surrounding words via attention. The idea of words as points in a semantic space carries over.

questions.prompt: Where does the chapter say TF-IDF breaks down? Select all that apply.
options: When synonyms matter, such as "car" and "automobile"
When there are millions of documents
When documents are very short
When word order changes meaning, such as "not good" against "good"
questions.explanation: The chapter lists synonymy, order-dependent meaning and very short documents. Scale is a strength: TF-IDF runs across millions of documents on a laptop in seconds.

questions.prompt: A retrieval system needs one vector per document. Why does the chapter point to sentence-transformers over averaging word vectors?
options: Averaging only works with 300-dimensional vectors.
Averaging can't be computed when a word is missing from the vocabulary.
Sentence-transformers are smaller than GloVe tables, so they cost less to store and serve.
Averaging drops order and is weak on short texts. Sentence-transformers are built for it.
questions.explanation: Procedure 27.5's limitation note says mean-pooling throws away order, and for short documents the signal is weak. A model trained for single-vector embeddings does better. Missing words are skipped in the average, not fatal.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 27.2 call transform() on the test set and never fit_transform()?
options: Fitting the vocabulary and IDF table on test data leaks test information into training.
fit_transform() is slower, so it is only used once.
transform() quietly adds the test words to the vocabulary, which fit_transform() doesn't.
fit_transform() returns a dense matrix, which the classifier rejects.
questions.explanation: The vocabulary and IDF weights are learned parameters. Learning them from test documents leaks test information. transform() uses the training vocabulary only, so unseen test words are ignored, not added.

questions.prompt: What is Procedure 27.1's common mistake?
options: Lemmatising before tokenising
Not applying the identical function to test data and new documents
Keeping punctuation tokens
Removing stopwords before lowercasing, so capitalised stopwords slip through
questions.explanation: The procedure says to wrap preprocessing in one function and call it everywhere, never inline the steps twice. Mismatched preprocessing is the text version of train/serve skew.

questions.prompt: Why does Procedure 27.3 put the vectoriser and the classifier in one Pipeline?
options: So the vocabulary is shared across all folds.
So cross-validation refits the vectoriser inside each fold
Because LogisticRegression can't read sparse matrices otherwise.
Because Pipelines train faster than separate steps.
questions.explanation: The procedure bundles preprocessing, vectorising and the model so cross-validation handles the whole thing correctly. Each fold fits its own vocabulary on its own training part, which avoids leakage. Sharing one vocabulary across folds is the leak.

questions.prompt: In Listing 27.5, what does doc_embedding return for a text whose words are all missing from the GloVe table?
options: The vector for the <unk> token
An error, because np.mean of an empty list fails
A zero vector of length dim
The mean of the whole embedding table
questions.explanation: vectors is empty, so the conditional returns np.zeros(dim). The guard exists because np.mean of an empty list would give NaN with a warning. GloVe has no <unk> vector in this code.

questions.prompt: On the four-category 20 Newsgroups task, which representation scored higher, and by about how much?
options: Averaged GloVe-50, by about 7.5 macro-F1 points
TF-IDF, by about 20 macro-F1 points
They tied within 0.5 points
TF-IDF, by about 7.5 macro-F1 points
questions.explanation: TF-IDF scored 0.9074 and mean-pooled GloVe-50 scored 0.8327, a gap of 0.0747. Same split, same classifier, same evaluation.

questions.prompt: Why does the chapter say averaged embeddings lost on this task?
options: 50 dimensions is too many for logistic regression to fit.
GloVe's vocabulary is missing most of the topic words, so documents became zero vectors.
Embeddings can only be used with neural networks, not logistic regression.
Averaging blurs a few topic words like nhl into many generic ones. TF-IDF keeps them.
questions.explanation: A 200-word document with three topic nouns becomes a vector dominated by the other 197 words. TF-IDF's sparse, exact-word features keep that signal. GloVe's 400,000-word vocabulary covers these words, and logistic regression handles 50 features easily.

questions.prompt: A team must route support tickets to one of five product teams. Each team's tickets mention distinct product names and error codes. A colleague wants averaged embeddings because they are more modern. What does the chapter suggest?
options: Use bag of words without IDF, since product names are rare.
Start with TF-IDF, which suits a clear vocabulary, and measure both on one split before choosing.
Use averaged embeddings, since they are a strict upgrade over TF-IDF.
Skip both and fine-tune a transformer, since classical text methods are now obsolete.
questions.explanation: The chapter's mental model says "smarter representation" doesn't mean better, and measuring both is the only way to know. Product names and error codes are exactly the specific vocabulary TF-IDF preserves. Embeddings are a different tool, better for semantic similarity.

bookExercises.prompt: Write the TF-IDF formula and explain, in one sentence, why a word appearing in every document in the corpus gets a weight of exactly zero.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: TF-IDF(word, doc) = TF(word, doc) × IDF(word), where IDF(word) = log(N / df(word)). A word appearing in every one of the N documents has df = N, so IDF = log(N/N) = log(1) = 0, and any TF value multiplied by zero is zero. The word contributes nothing to the document's vector, regardless of how often it appears within any single document.

bookExercises.prompt: State the one-sentence rule for when to call `.fit_transform()` versus `.transform()` on a `TfidfVectorizer`, and what goes wrong if the rule is violated.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Call `.fit_transform()` only on training data. It learns the vocabulary and IDF table, then transforms in one step. Call `.transform()` only on test/new data, reusing the vocabulary and IDF already learned from training. Calling `.fit_transform()` on test data re-learns a new vocabulary/IDF from the test set itself, which leaks test-set statistics into the pipeline and typically also produces a differently-shaped matrix than the one the trained classifier expects.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 27.6 and Listing 27.7's measured results (macro-F1 0.9074 vs. 0.8327 on the same 4-category split), explain in your own words why TF-IDF outperformed mean-pooled GloVe-50 here, and describe one type of task where you'd expect the ranking to flip.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: TF-IDF outperformed mean-pooled GloVe-50 here (0.9074 vs. 0.8327 macro-F1) because this task's discriminating signal is specific vocabulary. Words like `nhl`, `orbit`, `3d`, `doctor` are highly diagnostic of their category, and TF-IDF preserves each of these as its own dimension with a large weight. Mean-pooling averages a document's ~200 word vectors into one 50-dimensional point, so the three or four topic-defining words get diluted by the other ~196 generic words in the average. The ranking would likely flip on a task needing genuine semantic similarity across different vocabulary, e.g. matching "the patient had a myocardial infarction" to "the patient suffered a heart attack," where TF-IDF sees zero word overlap but embeddings correctly see near-identical meaning.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 27.8's result for `king - man + woman` (top-5: queen, daughter, prince, throne, princess, with cosine similarities 0.861 down to 0.751), explain what the *gap* between the top result and the second result suggests about how unambiguous this particular analogy is in the embedding space.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The gap between `queen` (0.861) and the next result, `daughter` (0.768), is a substantial 0.093 in cosine similarity. For a 50-dimensional space where most word pairs have much smaller similarity gaps, this is a wide margin, suggesting the analogy is largely unambiguous. The arithmetic result sits clearly closer to `queen` than to any of the four next-nearest words, rather than being a near-tie the model got lucky on.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague argues "word embeddings are strictly better than TF-IDF because they capture meaning." Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say in response.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "This chapter's Worked Example measured the opposite on a real classification task. TF-IDF scored 0.9074 macro-F1 versus embeddings' 0.8327 on the same 20 Newsgroups split. Embeddings do capture semantic similarity that TF-IDF can't, which matters enormously for retrieval and paraphrase-matching tasks. But 'captures meaning' isn't the same as 'wins on every task.' When the actual signal is specific, discriminating vocabulary rather than paraphrase-level similarity, TF-IDF's sparse exact-word representation can be the stronger choice. The only way to know which applies is to measure both on the actual task."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 27.5's `doc_embedding` returns a zero vector when none of a document's tokens are in the embedding vocabulary. Explain one concrete way this could silently corrupt a downstream classifier's training data, and one way to detect it happening.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: If a document happens to contain zero tokens from the embedding vocabulary (e.g., it's mostly numbers, code, or a language the embedding table wasn't trained on), `doc_embedding` silently returns an all-zero vector, indistinguishable from any other document that legitimately embeds near the origin. A classifier trained on data containing several such zero-vector documents effectively learns "the zero vector means class X" if those particular documents happen to skew toward one class, a spurious pattern with nothing to do with content. Detecting it: count how many training documents produce an all-zero embedding before training, and flag or route to a fallback representation (e.g., TF-IDF) any document whose vocabulary coverage is below a chosen threshold.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about FastText's subword embedding approach. Explain why it can produce a reasonable vector for a word never seen during training (e.g., "unhappiness"), when GloVe and Word2Vec, both used in this chapter, cannot.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: FastText represents each word as the sum of vectors for its character n-grams (subwords) rather than one atomic vector per whole word. "Unhappiness", even if never seen as a complete token during training, decomposes into subwords like "un", "happi", "ness" that likely *were* seen inside other training words (e.g., "unhappy", "happiness", "sadness"). FastText can compose a reasonable vector from those learned subword pieces. GloVe and Word2Vec store one fixed vector per whole word learned during training. A word absent from the training vocabulary simply has no vector at all, with no mechanism to construct one from its parts.
